chunks: And he also narrated from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Zurārah, from one of the two of them, peace be upon them, who said:
I asked him about a menstruating woman with whom her husband has intercourse. He said: “There is nothing upon him; he should seek Allah’s forgiveness and not return to it.”

So these reports are to be understood as referring to when he did not know that she was menstruating. But if he knew that, then expiation is binding upon him according to what we have mentioned. No one may say that this interpretation is impossible, because if these reports were understood as referring to the state of forgetfulness, they would not have said, peace be upon them, that he should seek his Lord’s forgiveness for what he did, nor that he disobeyed his Lord. For it is not impossible to describe him as having disobeyed, and to urge seeking forgiveness, inasmuch as he was negligent in asking her whether she was menstruating or not, while knowing that if she were menstruating, intercourse with her would be forbidden to him. By this negligence he was disobedient, and seeking forgiveness became obligatory upon him, because he undertook what he was not secure from being reprehensible. What reveals the correctness of this interpretation is the previously mentioned report of Layth al-Murādī. He said: I asked Abā ʿAbdillāh, peace be upon him, about a man having intercourse with his wife while she was menstruating by mistake. So he qualified the question by stating that his intercourse with her occurred in the state of error, and he, peace be upon him, answered: “There is nothing upon him, though he has disobeyed his Lord.”

As for what he mentioned in the book regarding considering the days in distinguishing between the first, middle, and last parts, it is necessary. For if the maximum number of days is ten days, and he said that in its beginning there is one dīnār, in its middle half a dīnār, and in its end a quarter dīnār, then there must necessarily be something by which each of these days is distinguished from the others. They are distinguished only by what he mentioned: that they become three sections according to what he explained.

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: When the blood of menstruation has ceased from the woman and her husband wishes to have intercourse with her, then it is preferable for him to leave her until she performs ghusl and then have intercourse with her. But if desire overcomes him and patience until she finishes the ghusl becomes difficult for him, then he should instruct her to wash her private part and then he may have intercourse with her, and there is no hardship upon him in that.

key_terms.الْخَطَإِ: error or mistake, as opposed to deliberate action
key_terms.الْكَفَّارَةُ: the expiation due for a knowing violation
key_terms.دِينَارٌ: a dīnār, the monetary measure used for expiation
key_terms.طَامِثٌ: menstruating; in a state of menses
key_terms.فَرْجِهَا: her private part, to be washed before intercourse after cessation of blood
key_terms.يَسْتَغْفِرُ: he seeks forgiveness from Allah for the act

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on intercourse with a menstruating wife, and is expiation required in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This text discusses the legal ruling of intercourse with a menstruating wife, distinguishing between cases of ignorance or error and cases of knowing violation, in which expiation is due. It also explains the gradation of expiation across the beginning, middle, and end of menstruation, and mentions that after menstruation ends it is preferable to wait until ghusl before intercourse.
